title: Bubble Sort
body:
Walk the [[Array]] comparing each adjacent pair and swapping them if they are out of order.
One pass drags the largest element to the end (it "bubbles" up), so after $n$ passes
everything is in place. $O(n^2)$ average and worst, and it is a teaching example only:
nothing real uses it.

```java
void bubbleSort(int[] a) {
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
        boolean swapped = false;
        for (int j = 0; j < a.length - 1 - i; j++) {   // last i are already final
            if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) { swap(a, j, j + 1); swapped = true; }
        }
        if (!swapped) return;                          // already sorted, stop
    }
}
```

The `swapped` flag gives it an $O(n)$ best case on already-sorted input, which is the only
nice thing about it. On anything else it does far more swaps than [[Insertion Sort]], which
is $O(n^2)$ too but with much smaller constants because it shifts rather than swapping
repeatedly.

It is stable (equal elements never swap past each other) and in place, and neither fact
rescues it. When you need $O(n^2)$ to be acceptable, the array is small enough that
insertion sort is the better choice; when it is not, use [[Merge Sort]] or [[Quick Sort]].
